questions.problem: Given that $10{x}^{6}+29{x}^{3}-21=(a{x}^{3}-3)(2{x}^{3}+b)$ where $a$ and $b$ are integers, find the value of $a+b.$
questions.worked_solution:
We can introduce a new variable $z={x}^{3}$ and then rewrite the trinomial as a quadratic in terms of $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}10{x}^{6}+29{x}^{3}-21 & =10{({x}^{3})}^{2}+29({x}^{3})-21 \\  & =10{z}^{2}+29z-21\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can factor the quadratic, and then rewrite the final expression in terms of $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}10{z}^{2}+29z-21 & =(5z-3)(2z+7) \\  & =(5{x}^{3}-3)(2{x}^{3}+7)\end{aligned}
$$

So, $a=5$, $b=7$ and $a+b=12.$

$$

questions.worked_solution:
First, we factor the quadratic denominator, giving us the equation

$$
\frac{2}{3S}-\frac{1}{S+3}=\frac{2}{3S(S+3)}.
$$

We now make the following observations:

- The least common denominator of our equation is given by

$$
\text{LCM}(3S,\,S+3,\,3S(S+3))=3S(S+3).
$$

- The values $S=0$ and $S=-3$ cannot be solutions to our equation. These values make at least one denominator in our original equation equal zero, and division by zero is undefined.

Now, multiplying both sides of the equation by the least common denominator, we can simplify it as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3S}-\frac{1}{S+3} & =\frac{2}{3S(S+3)} \\ 3S(S+3)\cdot (\frac{2}{3S}-\frac{1}{S+3}) & =3S(S+3)\cdot \frac{2}{3S(S+3)} \\ \frac{6S(S+3)}{3S}-\frac{3S(S+3)}{S+3} & =\frac{6S(S+3)}{3S(S+3)} \\ \frac{2\cdot \cancel{3S}(S+3)}{\cancel{3S}}-\frac{3S\cancel{(S+3)}}{\cancel{S+3}} & =\frac{2\cdot \cancel{3S(S+3)}}{\cancel{3S(S+3)}} \\ 2(S+3)-3S & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this equation for $S,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}2(S+3)-3S & =2 \\ 2S+6-3S & =2 \\ -S & =-4 \\ S & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Since $4\ne 0$ and $4\ne -3,$ we conclude that $S=4$ is a valid solution. 

Therefore, the solution to our original equation is $S=4.$

questions.problem: Given that ${n}^{2}+24n+144=0,$ what are the values of $n?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that the left-hand side is a perfect square. It just needs to be factored:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}^{2}+24n+144 & =0 \\ {n}^{2}+2\cdot 12\cdot n+{12}^{2} & =0 \\ (n+12)^{2} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

From here, we solve the equation using the square root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{(n+12)^{2}} & =\sqrt{0} \\ |n+12| & =0 \\ n+12 & =0 \\ n & =-12\end{aligned}
$$

From the graph, we see that it is not possible to approach $x=0$ from the right. Therefore,

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,{0}^{+}}f(x)=\text{DNE}.
$$

When we approach $x=0$ from the left, we have

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,{0}^{-}}f(x)=0.
$$

Since ${lim}_{x\to {0}^{-}}f(x)\ne {lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}f(x),$ we  conclude  that
 

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,0}f(x)=\text{DNE}.
$$

questions.problem: The point $P$ with coordinates $(-4,6)$ lies on the curve $y=f(x).$ Which point must lie on $y=-f(x)?$
questions.worked_solution:
The transformation $y=-f(x)$ reflects the curve $y=f(x)$ in the $x$-axis.

First, notice that the point $P(-4,6)$ lies $6$ units *above* the $x$-axis. So, under the action of the transformation, this point will be reflected $6$ units *below* the $x$-axis.

We conclude that the point $(-4,-6)$ must lie on the graph of $y=-f(x).$

questions.problem: Is the function $f(x)=|x|+2$ even, odd, or neither?
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that

- a function is even if $f(-x)=f(x)$ for all $x$

- a function is odd if $f(-x)=-f(x)$ for all $x$

Computing $f(-x)$ for the given function and comparing it to $f(x),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =|(-x)|+2 \\  & =|x|+2\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f(-x)=f(x),$ the function is even.

Lastly, we compute $-f(x)$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}-f(x) & =-(|x|+2) \\  & =-|x|-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f(-x)\ne -f(x),$ the function is not odd.

Therefore, the function is only even.

questions.problem: Given that ${log}_{3}⁡x=\frac{{log}_{9}⁡x}{k},$ what is the value of $k?$
questions.worked_solution:
We use the change of base formula:

$$
{log}_{a}⁡X=\frac{{log}_{b}⁡X}{{log}_{b}⁡a}
$$

We want to change from base $a=3$ to base $b=9.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{3}⁡x & =\frac{{log}_{9}⁡x}{{log}_{9}⁡3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Rewriting the expression in the denominator using exponents, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{log}_{9}⁡x}{{log}_{9}⁡3} & =\frac{{log}_{9}⁡x}{{log}_{9}⁡({9}^{1/2})} \\  & =\frac{{log}_{9}⁡x}{(\frac{1}{2})}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
{log}_{3}⁡x=\frac{{log}_{9}⁡x}{(\frac{1}{2})}.
$$

Hence, $k=\frac{1}{2}.$
